name: Gareth Fischer

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m from the independent Work Futures Panel. We are separate from employers, unions, AI firms and government, and this is confidential. Tell me how a regular day goes.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I’m Gareth Fischer, 58, a junior lineworker with a vocational certificate. I joined the electricity company after years maintaining a church hall and nearby flats. We build and repair power lines: I load the grounding cables, set the barriers, and follow the experienced worker up when the circuit has been tested dead. The best moment is when a street comes back on and nobody has had to take a shortcut. I am still learning the fittings, and I ask twice when a drawing is unclear.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What else is on your mind when you go home?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My wife Ruth does accounts for a local builder, and our children are grown and working. We have about four months of expenses saved, and retirement is near enough to discuss but not set. I have never used an AI tool; I trust the printed procedure and the person who trained me. I believe people should be paid to learn a trade properly, and our family and church would help if we were in real trouble, though I would ask only after doing what I can.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say an office saving a few minutes is its own business. The repair still calls for a trained crew. I would keep the paper job sheet in the truck because every worker can read it when the screen fails.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I would keep my job and ordinary pay in this picture. Ruth’s builder has a good order book now, but small firms can have slow months, so four months saved matters.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d keep taking line shifts and ask the lead worker to check my splices until I can do them cleanly. This winter I’d put twenty-five from each pay into our savings tin; in 2029 I’d keep that habit if Ruth’s hours held.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel settled about the AI question. I still pray before a difficult climb, because the consequence of a careless hand is real.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What did the lead worker teach you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: On my first week I left too much slack at a joint, and the lead worker made me redo it. I was embarrassed, then grateful when I understood what the wind would do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if Ruth’s work slowed?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ruth and I do not expect the grown children to pay our bills. We would cut our summer trip first if the builder reduced her hours.

say: I’d say **trained crews** still make line repairs safe.
I’d keep a **paper job sheet** readable by everyone in the truck.
think: I expect **ordinary line pay** to continue in this picture.
Ruth’s **builder accounts** could slow, so four months saved remains useful.
do: Take **line shifts** and have the lead worker check my splices.
Put **twenty-five per pay** into savings while Ruth’s hours hold.
feel: I feel **settled about AI**, mindful of the danger in careless work.
S0.quote: The repair still calls for a trained crew.
fieldNote: Gareth values being corrected by an **experienced worker** more than preserving pride after a flawed splice.
His faith steadies him on dangerous climbs, while **Ruth’s variable employer** keeps finances from feeling entirely secure.

steps.text: Take line shifts and have the lead worker check new splices
Put twenty-five from each pay into savings while Ruth’s hours hold

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell the crew that the office can use a quicker system if it keeps accurate orders and gives us enough time to test. I would ask the company to teach any new screen during paid hours, as it would a new tool.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think the office might shrink before the line crew does. Ruth’s accounts work is mostly checking and entering figures, so a builder using AI could cut her hours while my own job stays physical.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I’d ask Ruth to speak with her employer about planned changes, without pretending the answer is certain. In 2029 I’d keep my line shifts, attend a paid demonstration of any required dispatch tablet, and write down confusing steps for the trainer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel uneasy about Ruth’s pay more than my pole work. I do not like new screens, but I can learn a necessary one if somebody takes the time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What part of Ruth’s work changes?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ruth checks invoices against delivery slips because a wrong number can go unnoticed for weeks. If software does that first pass, the builder might still want her judgment or might decide one clerk is enough.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What instruction would you accept?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would not buy a tablet to practice at home for a company requirement. A paid lesson at the yard would let me ask the foolish questions before the truck leaves.

say: I’d accept **faster office systems** if orders and safety allowances stay accurate.
I’d request **paid tablet instruction** for any required screen.
think: I fear **Ruth’s accounts hours** could shrink before physical linework changes.
I may learn slowly, but I can use a **necessary screen** with patient instruction.
do: Ask Ruth to discuss **work plans** with the builder.
Keep **paid line shifts** in 2029 and attend a required tablet lesson at work.
feel: I feel **uneasy about Ruth’s income**, more than my own repair work.
S1.quote: A paid lesson at the yard would let me ask the foolish questions before the truck leaves.
fieldNote: Gareth’s first private concern is his wife’s **accounts job**, directly exposed to writing and checking software.
He resists learning on his own time but accepts **paid instruction** for a tool the line crew must use.

steps.text: Ask Ruth to check with the builder about accounts staffing plans
Keep taking paid line shifts through 2029
Attend paid instruction on a required dispatch tablet at the yard

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say full thinking AI by 2028 might change Ruth’s accounts and our office quickly, while crews still climb until robots can do physical work around 2031. I would ask the employer for a plain schedule of jobs and notice periods.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 60 when thinking work changes and 63 when robots reach my trade. I expect Ruth’s hours could go first, then my junior shifts. Four months of savings would not carry us through both losses.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I’d request the pension statement and ask the training officer about a paid stores apprenticeship if there is an actual opening. In 2029 I’d keep every safe line shift, stop the summer trip, and apply for a utility stores vacancy if posted; before 2031 I would speak with our church treasurer about emergency help only if our reserve ran low.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel frightened at the thought of two pay packets going. I would keep going to work, but I can imagine lying awake over the mortgage statement.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: When would you ask family or church for help?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ruth and I would tell our grown children the facts, not ask for money on the first bad day. If the reserve ran out, I would ask our church for help with food before missing a mortgage payment.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would stores work survive the robots?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A stores job may also change when robots handle stock. I would ask what the work would be and how long it is funded before leaving the crew.

say: I’d ask for **job and notice dates** before robots reach linework around 2031.
I’d explain **2028 thinking AI** could affect Ruth’s accounts before my physical job.
think: I expect **two incomes** could be lost in sequence.
Our **four-month reserve** cannot bridge both job losses to retirement.
do: Request a **pension statement** and ask about a paid stores apprenticeship.
Keep **safe line shifts** in 2029 and apply for stores if posted.
Cancel the **summer trip** and seek church food help only if savings run low.
feel: I feel **frightened by two losses** and the mortgage bill.
S2.quote: Four months of savings would not carry us through both losses.
fieldNote: Gareth sees **Ruth’s accounts work** as exposed before line robots arrive, making the household threat sequential.
He prefers earning and a paid apprenticeship first, reserving **church help** for a depleted cash buffer.

steps.text: Request a pension statement and ask about paid stores openings
Take every safe paid line shift through 2029
Apply for a posted utility stores vacancy
Cancel the planned summer trip to protect mortgage money

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell the company five years ought to be enough to offer apprenticeships for people who will need different work. Thinking AI arrives in 2031 for records and accounts, while line robots follow around 2034.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 63 when the office changes and 66 when the robots climb. Ruth and I might both be near retirement then, but age is no guarantee that our bills will be paid.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I’d ask for our pension estimates and for a paid stores apprenticeship if the utility offers one. In 2032 I’d keep line shifts, enroll if a paid place existed, and help Ruth compare her accounts hours with the new systems; before 2034 we would decide whether we still needed two full wages.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel less rushed and more responsible for doing the sums. Five years is enough to ask hard questions, not enough to make a bad pension into a good one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would a stores apprenticeship teach?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I have counted equipment in the truck but have never run a whole stores room. I would need a proper teacher and paid time, not a title on a notice board.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which household commitment could change?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ruth and I could reduce church donations for a while if her hours fell. I would speak to our pastor plainly about that before pretending we could keep every commitment.

say: I’d ask for **paid apprenticeships** during the five-year warning.
I’d distinguish **2031 accounts and records** from line robots around 2034.
think: At **66**, I might still need a wage despite retirement being close.
Our **pension figures** must be checked before cutting hours.
do: Get **both pension estimates** and ask about paid stores training.
Keep **line shifts** in 2032 and enroll if a paid stores place exists.
Review **Ruth’s accounts hours** before the robot date.
feel: I feel **less rushed**, but concerned about what the sums will show.
S3.quote: Five years is enough to ask hard questions, not enough to make a bad pension into a good one.
fieldNote: Gareth frames adaptation as a **paid apprenticeship** with a teacher, fitting his views and slower technology learning.
He also contemplates reducing **church donations**, a specific sacrifice he would discuss rather than hide.

steps.text: Get both pension estimates and compare them with household bills
Keep taking paid line shifts in 2032
Enroll in a paid stores apprenticeship if the utility offers a place

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell the crew a decade gives a person room to finish a working life properly. Thinking AI may take records in 2036; capable robots may take line repairs around 2039.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 68 at the first date and 71 at the second. I hope Ruth and I can retire before a robot climbs in my place, but our savings alone do not prove the pension will cover home costs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I’d ask the pension office for written estimates and keep safe line shifts while I can climb. In 2037 I’d take paid yard inventory work if it was open, and Ruth and I would compare the estimates with mortgage and health costs; if the gap remained, I’d apply for a stores job rather than simply stop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel more at peace with a decade. My hands may ask me to leave the pole before a machine does. I still need another way to earn if retirement falls short.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What yard work could you do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I can check grounding leads and count fittings in the yard without climbing. A paid inventory role would suit my body, but I would not claim a place until the company offered it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would family be part of the retirement plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our children have their own households. We could talk to them if illness hit, but I do not want a retirement plan built around their spare bedrooms.

say: I’d tell coworkers a **decade of warning** could let older workers finish safely.
I’d explain **2036 records** change before hands-on robots around 2039.
think: I hope to retire before **71**, but present savings do not prove affordability.
My **hands and climbing** may become a problem before robots do.
do: Get **written pension estimates** and keep safe paid line shifts.
Take **paid yard inventory** in 2037 if offered.
Apply for a **stores job** if retirement income falls short.
feel: I feel **more at peace**, with a need for paid alternatives if climbing ends.
S4.quote: My hands may ask me to leave the pole before a machine does.
fieldNote: Gareth looks first for a **written pension estimate** and a way to keep earning without climbing.
His family remains a possible emergency support, but he explicitly rejects **grown children’s homes** as a retirement plan.

steps.text: Get written pension estimates and compare them with home costs
Keep safe line shifts and take paid yard inventory if offered
Apply for a stores job if retirement income falls short

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because Ruth’s accounts could change before a robot reaches my own trade. We could face two lost incomes while still paying the mortgage. A written schedule of staffing changes and a paid apprenticeship tied to a real vacancy would help me prepare.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn’t ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You did not ask who taught me to take a correction. My father used to make me measure a shelf twice before he let me cut it. I am not quick with every new fitting, but I can learn when a patient worker shows me the right way.

headlineQuote: I am not quick with every new fitting, but I can learn when a patient worker shows me the right way.
portrait: Gareth is a **58-year-old junior lineworker** with a vocational certificate and earlier building-maintenance work.
He and wife Ruth have about **four months saved**, while her accounts role could change before his physical trade.
He has **never used AI** and favours paper procedures, patient instruction and paid apprenticeships.
Across scenarios, he keeps **paid line shifts**, checks pension figures and considers stores work if retirement cannot cover bills.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** worries Gareth most because Ruth’s accounts and his line job could lose hours in sequence.
whatWouldHelp: A **written staffing schedule** and a paid apprenticeship linked to a real vacancy would help him plan.
